title: The 4 Boring Rules Behind 1,061 Interested Buyers in One Quarter (With Emails)
description: The 4 cold email rules behind 1,061 interested leads in one quarter, the data behind each, and copy-paste emails for every rule.
lead: This is the full 4 rules guide from the reel. For each rule you get why it works, exactly how to do it, and copy-paste emails you can use today. These are the same rules behind our January to March 2026 dashboard: 236,545 emails, 4,372 replies and 1,061 interested leads.
insider: These 4 rules ran every day on the campaign in the case study below: **236,545 emails from January to March 2026, 4,372 replies and 1,061 interested leads**, with open tracking off. About one in four replies was a buyer who wanted to talk. The rules are the easy part. The work is keeping the domains healthy, the lists clean, the follow-ups going and every reply answered fast, every single day, and that's what we do for clients.

blocks.text: Why boring rules beat clever tricks

Most people who say cold email is dead are breaking one of four basic rules. They send from a free Gmail address, they send the same email to everyone, they send one email and give up, or they answer replies a day later. None of these feel like big mistakes. Together, they cut your results by more than half.

The numbers in this guide come from [Hunter's State of Email Outreach 2026](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email), which looked at **31 million emails** sent by Hunter users in 2025. Each rule below has its own number from that report, so you can see what it's worth.

What to do
What the data says
rows: Send from a domain you own, not a free address
Hunter: 5.2% replies vs 2.5% from free addresses
Add two true facts about their business
Hunter: 5.6% replies with two custom details vs 3.6% with none
Send a short sequence of 3, not 1
Hunter: 6.8% replies with 3 emails vs 3.3% with 1

blocks.text: Rule 1: Send from your own domain

**Why it works:** a free address (like name@gmail.com) looks like a stranger, not a business. You also can't set up your own sending records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) on a free address. Hunter found emails from a **custom domain got 5.2% replies vs 2.5% from free addresses**. That's about twice the replies for the same work.

items: Buy 1-3 extra domains that look like your brand, for example **getacme.com** or **tryacme.com**. Don't send cold email from your main domain, so your normal email stays safe.
Create 2-3 inboxes per domain with real names, like **sarah@getacme.com**.
Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC for each domain. Your email provider has a step-by-step page for this (links in the resources below).
Warm up new inboxes for about 2-3 weeks before you start cold sending, and keep each inbox to a small number of cold emails a day.
Point each extra domain to your real website, so anyone who checks it lands somewhere real.

blocks.label: Rule 1 email: a simple first email from your new domain
blocks.text:
Subject: {{company}} + new customers

Hi {{first_name}},

I run {{your_company}}. We help {{type_of_business}} get more {{result}} without {{common_pain}}.

Last quarter we did this for a {{similar_business}}: {{one_real_result}}.

Worth a quick chat to see if it fits {{company}}?

{{your_name}}
{{your_title}}, {{your_company}}

blocks.label: Quick check
blocks.text: Send one email from your new inbox to a Gmail and an Outlook address you own. If it lands in spam, fix your SPF, DKIM and DMARC before you send anything else.
Rule 2: Two real details per person, about their business

**Why it works:** a detail shows you looked at them, not at a list. Hunter found emails with **two custom details got 5.6% replies vs 3.6% for emails with none**. Hunter's survey also found that **67% of decision makers** say personalization using public information makes them more likely to reply.
The key word is **business**. "I saw you like golf" is about the person. "I saw you opened a second location in Austin" is about their business, and it gives you a reason to write.

items: A new location, new product or new service on their website
A job post (hiring 3 sales reps means they want more sales)
A recent review, award or news story
What their website says they sell, and who they sell it to
The tool they use (shown on their site or in a job post)

blocks.label: Rule 2 email: two details, one question
AI prompt: find the two details for you
blocks.text:
Here is a company website and any notes I have: [PASTE WEBSITE TEXT OR URL + NOTES]

Find 2 true, specific facts about this company's business (not about the person). Good examples: a new location, a new service, a job post, a recent review, who they sell to.

For each fact, write one short line I can use in a cold email, under 15 words, in plain English.

Only use facts you can see in what I gave you. If you can't find 2, say so. Do not guess.
Rule 3: Send three emails, not one

**Why it works:** people are busy. Your first email often arrives at the wrong moment. Hunter found that **3 emails got 6.8% replies vs 3.3% for 1 email**, about twice the replies. Hunter also found the best sequences use **three messages in total**. Most replies still come from the first email, so make that one strong, and make each follow-up add something new.

head: Email
When
What it does
rows: The main email: their detail, one result, one small question
A new angle: a different problem you solve, or a short proof
The easy out: one line, a simple yes-or-no question

blocks.label: Rule 3 emails: follow-up 1 (day 3-4)
blocks.text:
Hi {{first_name}},

One more idea for {{company}}.

Most {{type_of_business}} we talk to also lose time on {{second_problem}}. For one client we {{what_you_did}}, and {{one_real_result}}.

Want me to send the 3 steps we used?

{{your_name}}

blocks.label: Rule 3 emails: follow-up 2 (day 7-8)
blocks.text:
Hi {{first_name}},

I don't want to fill your inbox, so this is my last note.

Is getting more {{result}} a priority for {{company}} right now, or should I check back next quarter?

{{your_name}}

blocks.label: Keep follow-ups in the same thread
blocks.text: Send follow-ups as replies to your first email, so they can see the whole story in one place. Keep each one shorter than the email before it.
Rule 4: Answer every reply fast, with one specific time

**Why it works:** when someone replies, they're thinking about your offer right now. An hour later they're in a meeting. A day later they've forgotten. ColdIQ, an outbound agency, wrote that after they cut their reply time **to under 15 minutes, meeting booking rates from positive replies went up by over 30%** ([ColdIQ](https://coldiq.com/blog/5-cold-email-lessons-from-scaling-to-65m-arr-with-instantly)).

The second half of the rule matters just as much: **offer one specific time**. "When works for you?" starts a back-and-forth that can take days. "Does Tuesday at 2pm Eastern work?" can be answered with one word.

items: Turn on phone notifications for replies in your sending tool, or forward replies to one inbox you check often.
Answer every reply within your working hours, ideally within 5-15 minutes.
Answer the question they asked first, in one or two lines.
Offer one specific day and time, with the time zone. Add your booking link as a backup, not as the main ask.
If they don't answer in 24 hours, send one short nudge in the same thread.

blocks.label: Rule 4 email: reply to "Interested, tell me more"
Rule 4 email: reply to "What does it cost?"
blocks.text:
Good question, {{first_name}}.

It depends on {{the_one_or_two_things_price_depends_on}}. Most {{type_of_business}} like {{company}} land between {{low}} and {{high}} a month.

I can give you an exact number in a 15-minute call. Does {{day}} at {{time}} {{time_zone}} work?

{{your_name}}

blocks.label: Rule 4 email: nudge after 24 hours of silence
blocks.text: Hi {{first_name}}, still want to grab 15 minutes? I can do {{day}} at {{time}} or {{day_2}} at {{time_2}} {{time_zone}}. Either one work?
Worked example: what the 4 rules are worth

Say you email **2,000 people** this quarter. Here is what Hunter's numbers suggest for two of the rules on their own. (Each number comes from a separate comparison in the report, so don't add them together.)

Now say your replies turn into interested buyers at the same rate as our quarter in the case study below: **1,061 interested out of 4,372 replies, about 24%**. Then 136 replies x 24% = about **33 interested buyers**, compared with 66 x 24% = about **16** from one email. Same list, same offer, twice the conversations. Rule 4 is what turns those buyers into booked calls.
Problem finder: which rule are you breaking?

blocks.text: Your weekly checklist

items: All cold email goes out from your own extra domains, never a free address
Every email has two true details about the person's business
Every new lead is in a 3-email sequence
Replies are answered within 15 minutes during working hours
Every reply that's interested gets one specific time to meet
You track replies, interested replies and booked calls each week

blocks.label: Bottom line
blocks.text: Cold email isn't dead. Lazy cold email is. Four boring rules, done every day, beat any clever trick.

faq.q: Can I send cold email from my main company domain?
faq.a: It's safer not to. Use 1-3 extra domains that look like your brand, so if something goes wrong, your normal business email isn't hurt.

faq.q: Do I really need to personalize every email?
faq.a: Two true business details is enough. Hunter found that lifted replies from 3.6% to 5.6%. An AI prompt (above) can find them in under a minute per company.
Not if each email is short, adds something new and the last one gives an easy way out. Stop after the third email if they don't reply.

faq.q: What if I can't answer replies within 15 minutes?
faq.a: Set phone alerts and keep ready-made replies (like the ones above) so each answer takes a minute. Even answering within the hour beats answering the next day.
